utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We convene today to hear the accused's Rule 98 bis submission. The Rule provides: "At the close of the Prosecutor's case, the Trial Chamber shall, by oral decision, and after hearing the oral submission of the parties, enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there's no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." The test to be applied is whether there's evidence upon which, if accepted, a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused. The test is not whether a Trial Chamber would, in fact, convict beyond reasonable doubt, but rather whether it could do so. Therefore, Mr. Karadzic, please bear in mind the following two points. First, as you may already know well, at this stage of the case the Trial Chamber is not to evaluate the credibility of witnesses or the strength and weaknesses of contradictory or different evidence. Second, the rule falls to be applied to each of the 11 counts in the indictment, not requiring the Chamber to be satisfied that there's evidence supporting each of the individual charges making up the counts of the indictment. Having said that, Mr. Karadzic, I give you the floor for your submission. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, this morning we're going to divide the work between myself and Dr. Karadzic. There are two counts in which our arguments are predominantly legal in nature and those are Counts 1 and 11. So I will be making the submission on our team's behalf for Count 1 at the beginning, and then at the end after Dr. Karadzic has addressed Counts 2 through 10 I will return and deal with Count 11. So at this time Dr. Karadzic hereby moves for a judgement of acquittal pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence on each of the 11 counts in which he's charged. Turning to Count 1, the guts of Count 1 can be found in paragraph 38 of the indictment, and that charges that in some municipalities - and there are seven listed in the bottom of that paragraph - between 31 March and 31 December 1992 the campaign of persecutions alleged in the indictment included or escalated to include conduct that manifested an intent to destroy in part the national, ethnical, and/or religious groups of Bosnian Muslims and/or Bosnian Croats as such. And this count is charged in violation of Article 4 of the ICTY Statute. That Statute defines genocide as being any of the following acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group as such. And those acts include killings causing serious bodily or mental harm and deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about the destruction of the group. It's been said that genocide is the crime of crimes. The intent to destroy the group makes genocide an exceptionally grave crime and distinguishes it from other serious crimes, such as persecution, where the perpetrator selects his victims because of their membership in a specific community but does not necessarily seek to destroy the community as such. And so genocide is not simply the sum of killings on the one hand, the actus reus, and expressions such as the Muslims should disappear on the other hand, that being part of mens rea, but instead genocide is a confluence of those acts and intent so that the killings can be said to be committed not only because of hatred or revenge but with the special intent to actually destroy the group or a significant part thereof. And our position as to Count 1 is simply that there was no genocide in the municipalities in Bosnia in 1992, and therefore there is no evidence upon which the Trial Chamber could conclude that Dr. Karadzic is guilty of genocide as charged in Count 1. You don't have to take our word for it. The International Court of Justice has held that there was no genocide in the municipalities in Bosnia in 1992. Ruling in the lawsuit by Bosnia against Serbia and Montenegro, the International Court of Justice held that the court is not convinced that the massive killings of members of the protected group were committed with the specific intent on the part of the perpetrators to destroy, in whole or in part, the group as such. This decision was made 15 years after these events, and in the interim five years from 2007 until today, 2012, the Prosecutor has presented no new evidence that would call into question this result. In fact, the evidence in this case affirmatively indicates that there was no genocide in the municipalities. Exhibit D2250 is a chart that was produced by the Prosecution's expert Ewa Tabeau, and it shows that in all of Bosnia 2.6 per cent of the Muslims were killed. This includes soldiers who died in battle and includes three and a half years of the war, not just 1992. It includes the 1995 killings in Srebrenica, which are reflected in the total for Bratunac municipality. So it's likely that the actual number of civilians who were killed as a result of war crimes is well under 2 per cent of the population. That's no genocide. Almost 60 per cent of the Jews in Europe were killed during the Holocaust and about 70 per cent of the Tutsis were killed during the Rwandan genocide. Now, the key to understanding the jurisprudence about the genocide in municipalities is simply that displacement does not equal destruction. And we can go back to the Genocide Convention itself. There was an amendment offered ironically by Syria which would have made displacement an act of genocide, and that amendment was voted down 29 to 5, ironically Yugoslavia voting in favour of the amendment. And so it evidences a clear intention on behalf of the drafters of the Genocide Convention that acts of displacement as opposed to destruction do not constitute genocide. In the Eichmann case in Israel in 1961, Eichmann was acquitted of genocide for acts which took place before 1941 because the court found that up until that time the Germans were intent on displacing and expelling the Jews, but after the invasion -- the attack by the Soviet Union in 1941 their programme changed and they became intent on destruction and killing and not allowing displacement. And therefore, Eichmann was convicted of genocide only for those acts which were directed at destroying the group and not displacing it. Let's look at the jurisprudence of genocide at the ICTY in the municipalities. The first case involved Goran Jelesic, a guard at the Luka camp in Brcko municipality, a person who was said to have called himself the Serb Adolf. The Trial Chamber in his case held that there was no evidence of a plan to destroy the Muslims in Brcko or elsewhere, and that Jelesic killed arbitrarily. The Appeals Chamber disagreed. They said that the existence of a plan was not required, that displays of randomness cited by the Trial Chamber did not negate genocidal intent, but they declined to reverse the Trial Chamber, finding that it was not in the interests of justice that Jelesic be tried for genocide and his acquittal stood. And I mention that Brcko is not among the seven municipalities in which genocide is charged in this case. The next occasion in which this Tribunal has examined the issue of genocide in the municipalities was the case of Dusko Sikirica, a case of three guards at the Keraterm camp in the Prijedor area, and in that case the judgement for -- motion for judgement of acquittal was granted by the Trial Chamber, and those killings included the infamous room 3 massacre at Keraterm and they found that that was not with the intent to destroy the group as such. The Trial Chamber said in the Sikirica case that while the Prosecution has adduced evidence which might suggest that the Bosnian Serb authorities' general political doctrine gave rise to a campaign of persecution against the non-Serb population in Prijedor, there is no evidence that this doctrine sought to promote genocide. The Sikirica case also dealt with two ways in which genocide could be committed, targeting a substantial number of people or targeting a selective number of individuals who comprised the leadership. And in that case it indicated that the targeting of a selective number of persons who by reasons of their special qualities of leadership within the group as a whole are of such importance that their victimisation would impact on the survival of the group as such, and they went on to find that there was no targeting of the leadership in such a way at Keraterm camp and that there was no evidence that the killing or disappearance of the people in those camp was based upon the special leadership or targeting of the special leadership, such as to destroy the group. And the same is true here. If you look at some of the major events in the Prosecution's case here, you can see why they were not committed with the intent to destroy the group. If you look at the Koricanske Stijene event, thousands of Muslims were transported towards Muslim territory when near the place Koricanske Stijene the -- there was a selection made of a few hundred of them or less than a few hundred of them, and that selection was based upon criteria or whether they fit into category 1, 2, or 3. Category 1 being combatants, people who had participated in the war according to them, those persons were taken off of the buses and killed. And the remaining thousands were taken to the Muslim territory. If there was an intent to destroy, then of course the object would have been to kill all of the Muslims or as many of them as they could. And if there was an effort to target the leadership, then the criteria for selection of those who were killed would have been based on those who were leaders in the community rather than those who were combatants and who could come back to fight again against the Bosnian Serbs. If you look at the system of prisoner exchanges, it flies in the face of genocide. Thousands of Bosnian Muslims were exchanged, were released during the course of 1992. Do you know how many Tutsis were exchanged for Hutus in Rwanda? Zero. Again, showing that there was no genocide in the municipalities in 1992. The next case in which the Tribunal dealt with the genocide in the municipalities was that of Milomir Stakic, the president of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor municipality. He was acquitted of genocide. The Trial Chamber said the Serbs had the means to commit genocide if they so intended. Had the aim been to kill all Muslims, the structures were in place for this to be accomplished. The Trial Chamber notes that while approximately 23.000 people were registered as having passed through Trnopolje camp, the total number of killings in Prijedor municipality probably did not exceed 3.000. The Trial Chamber in Stakic was not satisfied that anyone had the special intent to destroy the Muslims or Croats as a group and they specifically discussed the strategic goals, which is Exhibit P781 in this case and found that they called for separation and not destruction. The Court concluded that there was insufficient evidence in this case to prove that a genocidal campaign was being planned at a higher level. Now, here's what the International Court of Justice said about the strategic goals. The applicant's argument does not come to terms with the fact that an essential motive of much of the Bosnian Serb leadership to create a larger Serb state by war or conquest if necessary did not necessarily require the destruction of the Bosnian Muslims and other communities, but their expulsion. The 1992 objectives, particularly the first one, were capable of being achieved by the displacement of the population and by territory being acquired. The Appeals Chamber in Stakic affirmed the acquittal for genocide and rejected the Prosecution's appeal. It found that the evidence could reasonably be seen as consistent with the conclusion that the Trial Chamber drew that the appellant merely intended to displace but not destroy the Muslim group. And it pointed to some evidence to the contrary, such as Stakic's statement that Bosnian Muslims who did not take part in hostilities would be permitted to return to Prijedor after the war. And we have similar evidence in this case, including Dr. Karadzic's order of the 13th of June, 1992, Exhibit D101, in which he annulled any documents that had been signed by Muslims or Croats relinquishing their property before leaving municipality. Now, the next case in which the Tribunal dealt with genocide in the municipalities was the Milosevic case, and in the Rule 98 bis motion for judgement of acquittal, the Trial Chamber found that there was evidence from which genocide in the municipalities could be inferred. As we know, that case never proceeded to a final judgement because of the death of President Milosevic. The decision took place in June of 2004 preceding the Appeals Chamber's decision in Stakic and also the International Court of Justice judgement in 2007. Even in Stakic and Brdjanin and Krajisnik, which I'm about to discuss, the Rule 98 bis motions were denied only to find an acquittal at the end of the case. All of those rulings took place before the decisions of the International Court of Justice, which firmly established that no genocide took place in the municipalities and did so on a lower burden of proof of the preponderance of the evidence rather than whether there is evidence capable of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. And so you may be asking yourself why you should grant a motion for acquittal at this stage on Count 1 rather than waiting until the end of the case and deciding on the final judgement. And the answer is that, first of all, you have the decision now of the International Court of Justice, but most importantly part of the right to a fair trial that Rule 98 bis is designed to guarantee to the accused is the protection from having to defend himself from overcharging or charges which are not warranted in light of the evidence and the jurisprudence; and to allow an accused to focus the resources, scarce as they are, to him and compared to the Prosecution on crimes for which there is actually evidence which could sustain a conviction. You know, I am paid 75 euros an hour for my work here. If I spend one hour on genocide in the Defence case, just one hour, that -- those resources can be used to feed two children in Africa for a month. And so it's incumbent upon the Trial Chamber, in our submission, to address the issue at this stage and to determine really whether in light of all this jurisprudence and the evidence that you've heard the case for genocide in the municipalities should go forward. I turn now to the decision in the Brdjanin case. As you know Radoslav Brdjanin was the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the highest regional figure within Bosnia, and in his case the Trial Chamber also acquitted him of genocide in the municipalities. It found that there was -- from the summer of 1992, the Bosnian Serb forces controlled the territory of the ARK, as shown by the fact they were capable of mustering the logistical resources to forcibly displace tens of thousands of Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, resources which, had such been the intent, could have been employed in the destructions of all the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats of the ARK. The Trial Chamber in the Brdjanin case examined much of the same evidence that you've heard in this case, the killings at Koricanske Stijene, killings and treatment of prisoners at Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, and acts in the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc, which are charged as some of the seven municipalities in which genocide is alleged to have occurred. And in the Brdjanin case the Trial Chamber heard many of the same utterances that you've heard, intercepts, public speeches, and they noted that some of the accused's utterances are openly nasty, hateful, intolerable, repulsive, and disgraceful, but whilst these utterances strongly suggest the accused's discriminatory intent; however, they do not allow for the conclusion that the accused harboured the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats of the ARK. In the Brdjanin case they also talked about the notion of escalation to genocide, which is also charged in our indictment. And they found no evidence of escalation to genocide in the ARK, and that's at paragraph 982, and there was also no evidence of escalation to genocide in this case. The last case in which genocide was dealt with in the municipalities at this Tribunal involves the prosecution of Momcilo Krajisnik, who was the president of the Assembly and a closest associate of Dr. Karadzic. And he was charged with genocide on a national level. The Trial Chamber found no intention to destroy the group. They said: The Chamber does not find that any of these acts were committed with the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Croat ethnic group as such. And those acts include virtually all of the acts that are charged in this case, including the killings at Karakaj technical school in Zvornik and the Susica camp in Vlasenica. They contain the same utterances and documents Variant A and B, the six strategic goals, Dr. Karadzic's October 1991 speech before the Assembly, and the same intercepted conversations. So all of this jurisprudence leads inescapably to the conclusion that no genocide in the municipalities in Bosnia took place in 1992. And I would point out that genocide, as charged in this indictment, is not an inchoate crime. He is not charged with incitement to genocide or conspiracy to commit genocide. So it has to be established that a genocide actually took place in order for there to be evidence upon which you could convict Dr. Karadzic of Count 1. And I point out that the genocide in Count 1 does not include the killings in Srebrenica, which are the subject of Count 2. The Prosecution has not brought anything new in this trial that would cause you to question whether you ought to depart from this overwhelming weight of the jurisprudence. Despite having millions of documents in its possession, entire collections of Bosnian Serb military and political entities, intercepted conversations, minutes of secret meetings, there is simply no evidence that genocide was committed in the municipalities in Bosnia in 1992. Now, last week at the United Nations Security Council, Prosecutor Brammertz criticised the president of Serbia for denying the genocide in Srebrenica. He said that recent comments made by the newly elected president of Serbia who denied that genocide occurred in Srebrenica in July 1995 are not acceptable and contravene the legal and factual findings of the ICTY and the International Court of Justice. And likewise, the Prosecution's continuing efforts to claim that genocide occurred in the municipalities in Bosnia in 1992 contravenes the legal and factual findings of the ICTY and the International Court of Justice. The Prosecutor went on to say that such rhetoric is a backwards step, aggravates the victims' suffering and jeopardises the fragile process of reconciliation in the former Yugoslavia. And likewise, the Prosecution's claims that genocide occurred in the municipalities in Bosnia in 1992, in light of all the jurisprudence, does no service to this Court or to the people of the former Yugoslavia. There's no doubt that the suffering during the war in Bosnia was immense and that many crimes were committed. But there's no evidence upon which the Trial Chamber could conclude that there was an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats in the municipalities in 1992, and therefore Dr. Karadzic is entitled to a judgement of acquittal on Count 1 of the indictment. I will now turn the proceedings over to Dr. Karadzic for a discussion of the remaining Counts 2 through 10. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, the French translation has been just concluded. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all. I would like to touch upon each and every count, but within the framework of Rule 98 bis. First of all, I would like to pay tribute to our learned colleagues from the Prosecution because they made a huge effort to make some kind of an indictment out of nothing. What I'm going to say does not have to do with their incapability or their negligence, but simply the fact that there wasn't material to make this indictment look better. The entire indictment is based upon a few things that were stated but not proven. That is why I'm going to deal with them first because they are the basis of the entire indictment, practically all the counts. So the entire indictment against me is founded on my alleged intent or that we Serbs intended to get rid of Bosnian Muslims and Croats from the territories that they -- where they had a right to live. The Prosecution did not prove the basic part of this allegation; namely, that we lastingly wanted to remove Bosnian Muslims and Croats from these territories because the Prosecution was also aware of the fact that temporary removal - or whatever word we use in this context - of jeopardised civilians in this area is something that is both desirable and indispensable on the basis of our law of self-defence and self protection. So these civilians had to be removed from combat areas. We expected Count 1 to go on for longer so we did not complete our technical preparations, but anyway we saw this law here and we saw that this linguistic confusion that is due to imprecise translations in terms of what expert moves, shift, move, et cetera. All of that contributed to a misunderstanding of what had been done by certain commands or certain civilian leadership in certain municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you need a short break, the Chamber is minded to take a five-minute break for your preparation if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That would be good. Thank you.
