utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. I note that your presentation material can be viewed through e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm not sure that it's going to be brilliant, but we'll try to make do as my explanations go along. In some stage we should have reached agreement on what was envisaged by our legislation. Our Law on All People's Defence prescribes the following. Like in other countries, if there is a natural disaster, if there is a hurricane on the US coast, there has to be evacuation. And the same goes for the Law on National Defence in our country. No one says there that they are not going to go back. That goes without saying. Also, no document issued by the state authorities or the political authorities of Republika Srpska did not deny the right of persons who fled from combat areas to return. On the contrary, from the 11th of April, 1992, until the end of September 1992, we signed five or six agreements that define how the population would be evacuated, removed, how this would be done in a lawful, regulated manner, accompanied by the police, and of course the right to return was included. The birthday of this alleged intention to remove permanently - I repeat this word, permanently - was never proven, no proper attempt was even made to do that, and the Prosecution claims that this happened in October 1991. We saw here that all of 1991 was beset by political struggles in which the Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a rather conservative position as they tried to preserve Yugoslavia as a whole and Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole within Yugoslavia. It's not the Serbs that are the first to mention separation and division; it was Mr. Izetbegovic. Then in 1991 we accepted two of the main proposals of the largest Muslim parties: Izetbegovic's for an independent Bosnia transformed into three republics; and Zulfikarpasic's, that we give up on regionalisation and three republics but that we stay in Yugoslavia. So even the interpretation of my sentences that were mutilated could not prove this, that we wanted to remove them and that we wanted to remove them permanently. What was particularly not proven was that we denied their right to return. There's another thing that the Prosecution believed that went without saying but they did not prove it. The Prosecution views the following as a fundamental precondition for implementing Serb strategic objectives, that is, war and violence. However, that is not correct and that was not proven. On the contrary, what was proven was that Serb objectives were recognised by the international community, Serb fears were taken into account, Serb fears of a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that considerably before the war there were bilateral, trilateral political talks in which the European Community took part as well, and they proposed a concept of Bosnia that would resemble a Balkan Switzerland; that is to say, consisting of several entities. This Serb objective was recognised before the war and throughout 1992 until the beginning of 1993. There were discussions and agreements and the Serb side acted bona fide in all of this. It was obvious that these objectives could be attained without going to war. We have admitted into evidence documents from February and March from the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is shown unequivocally there that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be multiethnic. Unequivocally we see that Bosniaks and Croats would take part in political life proportionately, as would be the case with the Serbs in the Muslim and Croat units. So our aspirations and our objectives were recognised in all the plans before the war, during the war, and after the war, all the way up to Dayton; that is to say, this was not proven, that we thought that a precondition for this was going to war. Also, it is not logical because the Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina is the largest. It had not prepared for war at all. It relied on the protection of the Yugoslav state and the Yugoslav People's Army. And, finally, witnesses here, primarily Robert Donia, said that they knew that I was against war. Also, we saw that on the 8th of March, 1992, Mr. Vance informed Mr. Genscher - and that is not under seal, that is a public document - this sentence, Dr. Karadzic wishes to avoid war at all costs. The Prosecution did not prove that crimes to otherwise happen in all civil wars happened in our civil war because there was a joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution failed to prove that this was an overarching joint criminal enterprise, by virtue of the fact that they can indicate some things that happened only in a few out of over 60 municipalities in Republika Srpska. Dr. Mujadzic, a Prosecution witness, confirmed here that in places where Muslims had less than 50 per cent, 20 or 30 per cent, they did not have any problems. And the page reference is from 20.000 and further on, 20.500, 600, 700, 650 to 720, Dr. Mujadzic confirmed that I was against war, that I wanted to avoid war, that he wanted to avoid war, and that that would have been a good thing. And he confirmed that terrible things happened in the valley of the Sana River that was strategically important both for the Yugoslav People's Army, later on the Army of Republika Srpska, and for the Muslim army, clearly showing that their strategic objective was to take at least the left bank of the Sana River and annex all of that to the Cazin Krajina. So these are things that were clearly proven here, and on the other hand there is no evidence to the contrary that would confirm that this joint criminal enterprise was set up, that I took part in its establishment. On the contrary, up until the very last day, until the 1st of April, the entire Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, its entire political being was involved in establishing organs of authority in the new organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecution states that these organs were established with a view to attaining these objectives; however, these organs were envisaged by the Lisbon Agreement as well and any other agreement. And their accelerated establishment was aimed at preventing chaos, not creating chaos. The Prosecution did not even take into account an adjudicated fact from another trial in this Tribunal, and that Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that until 1992 I took into account the interests of the Croats and Muslims until the 14th of February, 1992, that is. In paragraph 907 there is a reference to my speech. I am going to read that. Paragraph 907 of the trial judgement in the Krajisnik case, that's the reference, actually. It says: [In English] "It is up to each individual to do his part of the job. We shall also talk about that today, but I have to say that we must be wise, unified, dedicated in order to take the last drop of power in our hands, in a humane way of course, carry it out in a humane way, a just way towards both Muslims and Croats who live there, that is particularly important, that there would be no fleeing from our areas." [Interpretation] And in paragraph 908, it states: [In English] "At each stage in early 1992, respect for the interests of other peoples was still being expressed by Karadzic, as separation and homogenization were not yet the declared aim of the nascent leadership." [Interpretation] If that is so, then it was the duty of the Prosecution to set a new date when this alleged intent came into the forefront that I am being charged with. One would see that on the 11th of April I signed an agreement with the UNHCR. On the 22nd of April I issued a platform suggesting that territories taken by force be not recognised and that peace be secured as soon as possible, as well as the return of all. On the 3rd of May we have seen here and we have the source from the newspaper, my press conference where in response to a question of whether there will be displacement, I said that we do not foresee or recommend displacement of the population but reciprocal protection of minority rights. And this applied throughout 1992 when I fought that all the Muslim and Croats be protected, that they have their representatives. And when I was elected I sought the Assembly to elect the prosecutors. So there will not be a new birthday for this alleged intent on my part, because that alleged intent did not actually exist on my part or on my side. Now I would like to deal with the Count 2, which is genocide as it relates to Srebrenica. Already in paragraph 1 of the indictment the Prosecution states something that they have not proved because they did not present any evidence that I, together with others, planned, instigated, ordered, and/or aided and abetted genocide in Srebrenica. Quite the contrary. There is evidence in case that there was no intent for the Army of Republika Srpska to enter Srebrenica, but they actually did that after the town was abandoned by the 28th Division and by the population. We can even see here statements by insiders and others who were familiar with these events and we even have statements by the perpetrators, those who killed prisoners of war, that they did not know anyone who had the intent of destroying the Muslims in Srebrenica and neither did they have that intent. Now, the Prosecution remains by its assertion, unsubstantiated by anything, that I either planned or intended to, and even if I did not perhaps intend to, perhaps alternatively I could have and should have foreseen that some of the members of the joint criminal intent could have committed genocide if our particular conduct or fighting did continue. The question of military action around Srebrenica was a military matter and it was very justified because it was insupportable to tolerate continuous attacks from Srebrenica. The question of entering Srebrenica became relevant on the night between the 9th and the 10th of July. We saw here that I was informed that they can enter and that I did agree to that and did order for them to act in the most humane way possible. Thus, there was no intent even to enter Srebrenica and never mind plans, according to the Prosecution, that these plans were created during the days of the attack. So there is awareness that there were no plans before the attack, but allegedly during the attack this decision appeared to be made. They did not present any evidence as to who made the decision on the genocide and the killing in general. When? At which point in time? On the -- well, we will come back to the question of killing, but on the matter of the alleged forcible displacement or deportation of the population from Srebrenica, it has been proved beyond any doubt here that the Serbian army did not have any combat contacts in Srebrenica and its vicinity and it did not have any combat contact with the 28th Division and did not have any contact with the population before this contact occurred in Potocari where the population, at the instigation of their own authorities, went to seek shelter. The Prosecution during the presentation of their case put in a lot of effort, fighting for every hour and every minute, in order to prove that Mladic or the Serbian side planned or were prepared to evacuate the civilian population before that population actually expressed its own will about that. It is more than obvious that no deportation was planned. It was shown that the evacuation of the population was something that was favoured by the local authorities in Srebrenica and the central authorities this Sarajevo, and that the central authorities in Sarajevo sought intervention via the United Nations for the Serbian side to permit the evacuation. The United Nations conveyed that request through General Nicolai and Colonel Karremans to Mladic, but Mladic did not grant this even then until representatives of the Muslim population themselves came and stated exactly what it is that they wished. Thus, the Prosecution did invest a lot of effort in this and I think that they should be recognised for these efforts to prove that there was some actions around the evacuation that were done some 10 or more hours before the 10th of July. But already in the evening of the 11th of July, it was clear what the Muslim side wanted. On July 12th no preparatory actions were carried out other than just information as to where vehicles could be obtained from. After that we can also see that the evacuation of the population was underway in the direction in which they wished to go and it is not said anywhere or there is no action indicating that they would not return and that they would not come back to their town again. It is very clear from a document of mine of the 11th of July, where I appoint the civilian representatives and ordered the formation of the organs of authority, that this refers only to the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica. And we can all remember that the forming of ethnically defined municipalities was one of the topics before the war broke out and after the war broke out, so that each community could feel safe. They were able to form their own authorities, have their own positions and manage the affairs of their own community completely independent from other ethnic communities and pursuant to their common laws. No one knew nor could anyone have foreseen, since as there is no evidence that I have done something actively, I am being charged with not foreseeing what would happen. Who could have foreseen that the 28th Division was going to leave the enclave much earlier than they needed to because they had more manpower than the Serbian army did? Who could have foreseen that the entire population would leave their homes? No one could have foreseen that. And it was not possible to plan, it was not possible to foresee the conduct of the commander, such as Oric and others who had their own concept and ideas about how to involve the Serbs in Srebrenica, get them to come in. Now, let us look at how witnesses described these matters relating to the evacuation. Let us look at Witness Kingori's testimony that he told General Mladic that he would obtain vehicles for the evacuation. We can see here the testimony of Nikolic about how they arrived, soldiers of the United Nations arrived, asking that the evacuation be speeded up. This is from the testimony of Witness Rutten before the Dutch parliamentary inquiry. We also saw evidence that the Dutch defence ministry was also in favour of the evacuation being carried out. None of the Serbs or the foreigners considered this to be a permanent thing and there was no indication that this would be a permanent thing. This is KDZ084. We will recall that he testified that on the 13th up until the early evening everything seemed quiet and it was assumed that there would be an exchange of prisoners and that nothing happened until the incident in Kravica. The Prosecution invested considerable efforts to prove that the killing in the Cerska Valley happened before the Kravica incident. However, this did not succeed because Prosecution witnesses confirmed here that the incidents in Cerska did not occur on the 13th but on the 17th or later because the people who were exhumed there were seen alive on the 17th. Prosecution Witness prominent investigator confirmed that in places where there was a greater military or police presence, such as in Potocari, there was no killing, while in the town where old people and reserves were maintaining law and order, there were killings, personal vendettas, calling people out from specific villages. Thus, wherever state authorities were present, there were no crimes. In the same way, the organs that we were speedily forming throughout 1992, for which the Prosecution claims were formed in order for us to achieve our criminal objectives actually clearly indicates that the greater the organised degree of the authorities, the smaller percentage of crimes and insecurity was recorded. And it's the other way around, where the present -- the presence of the state was possible in such an awful situation. Things could have been much worse. I'm afraid, Your Excellencies, that the Muslim propaganda about the events, the causes, the consequences, the corps, the number of victims was something that influenced the Prosecution. They completely took in the propaganda of Muslim extremists who were distorting things, not only as to the causes and the consequences but also in regard to precise data about the number of victims. Regardless of that, even if deportations did occur, the Prosecution did not present any proof about my knowledge, never mind about my possible participation or contribution. The Defence holds that the Prosecution, in the presentation of their case, presented evidence that there was no prior plan but that it was a matter of fulfilling the wishes of the Muslim population, the Muslim government, and the international bodies, including the Dutch government to a certain extent. But there was no evidence about my knowledge and even less about my active participation in any of the acts that I'm being charged with in relation to the evacuation, or rather - as it is said in the indictment - forcible displacement. Looking at it more broadly, the Prosecution ascribes to me the responsibility of having, in March 1992, formed the intent to capture Srebrenica and to commit crimes there; again, within the framework of a comprehensive joint criminal enterprise with a purpose of permanent removal, et cetera, et cetera. The Prosecution is probably relying on directive number 7. Without going into who and how created directive number 7 at the moment, without even going into the fact that directive number 7 is not an executive document and that it was followed by directive number 7.1, which does not contain any elements that would be indicative of a criminal act, we have succeeded during the Prosecution case to prove that directive number 7 resulted in none of the consequences that are ascribed to it. The humanitarian aid did not cease and the Prosecution witness testified here that she uses children as a criterion of the situation in an area and she saw a lot of children in the streets of Srebrenica, which meant there was no shelling, that the children were well nourished and healthy, which meant to her that there was sufficient medicine and food. And we have seen that convoys ceaselessly travelled and convoys were even approved for the 11th of July, arriving on the 13th. On that point, we have the testimony of General Obradovic who says that was intended for the civilian population and it did not matter how the fighting would end, in whose favour. However, the Prosecution probably neglected the fact that in 1993 I stopped our army at the boundaries of the enclave and forbade investigations. General Milovanovic spoke about that. I forbade investigations, lest personal elements interfere with this because people had been killing each other for centuries before that and the Serbs were the main victims until April 1993. So in April 1993 I forbade Serbs from entering Srebrenica and I forbade any investigations that might lead to incidents. As regards killings, first of all, the Prosecution has failed to show a single document that would indicate anybody's intention to carry out unlawful murders, anyone's intention to kill prisoners of war. In no aspect did the Prosecution show that there had been killings of civilians or that there had been intent to kill civilians. However, as regards the killing of prisoners of war, the Prosecution has not proven that anything happened before the Kravica incident. Concerning the Kravica incident we have seen that it occurred because one of the prisoners in a relaxed atmosphere, which the guards supported, snatched a weapon on board a bus, started shooting, and created chaos. We have also seen and heard that a certain number of Muslim soldiers falsely surrendered and then activated a bomb making a suicide bombing. That also contributed to the chaotic course of events. The repenting perpetrators who admitted to the killings of prisoners of war confirmed that the thought never crossed their minds of exterminating Muslims as a group. They confirmed that an unidentified lieutenant-colonel complained that they were dangerous, unpredictable, and impossible to control, and Erdemovic testified here that he had not discuss it with anyone except after crossing into Serbia where he discussed it with the former deputy commander, Kremenovic and he was unable to discuss it with anyone who could have told it to his superior commander. And that phenomenon, the next level, the immediate superior was not able to know many of these things. We will see that Pelemis himself did not know because Erdemovic did not dare to speak to anyone who was able to inform the commanders. We have equally seen and heard that silence reigned everywhere. Everyone kept their mouths shut about the events that happened on the 14th and later, and the question arises: How could the president of the republic who had his hands full all day, every day, possibly know something that was not known even to the people in the chain of command, in the very area where the events occurred? Your Excellencies, is this a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we'll take a break now but I'm asked to remind you of two things. First of all, to stick very closely to the requirements of the actual purpose of these proceedings. It's not a final submission. You should be submitting and not commenting about the matters which are capable of mounting to proof, and not whether or not they in fact amount to proof. That's a distinction which is very important at this stage of the proceedings. You must be careful also to distinguish between comment, which you have been doing on a widespread basis, although we have let you continue, and a submission. You will have seen the difference between comment and submission when you observed the way that Mr. Robinson addressed the Court in respect of the matters that he dealt with. He didn't make a single comment; he made submissions. And it would be very useful for us, and indeed for yourself, if you could follow his professional example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The issue of the events in Srebrenica which is dealt with in Count 2, genocide, as well as in counts that deal with municipality by municipality, I should like to remind you, since it has not been proven that there had been plans or intent and especially that there had been any knowledge on my part, let us look at all the things the witnesses have said about it. We have all the intercepts, all the documents, the testimony of people who spent the critical days with me, the days when the events in Srebrenica happened, and there is not a shred of evidence that I was even informed, let alone aware of the killings or deportations. But since we are dealing with Count 2 now, there were no plans, no knowledge, no reports about that, nor was the Prosecution able to present a single piece of evidence. On the contrary, we see that even international witnesses have shown that it was not proven. In fact, they have shown exactly the opposite. It has also been proven that there had been opportunistic killings driven by personal motivations such as revenge, and the indictment also features military targets and other operations as parts of the joint criminal enterprise. All this cannot be repeated all the time, but it is repeated in the indictment. My responsibility for the events in Srebrenica has been -- has not been proven in any way. It is my assertion that it was not genocide and it is up to the Prosecution to prove what actually happened. Who killed POWs and for what reasons? What matters is that the Prosecution has not established one of the most important facts; namely, the number of victims. The number is part of the game which is making the people there miserable and is creating a fertile ground for future hostilities. The Prosecution has not proven the number that is being played around with in the public domain. And there are no elements based on which the Trial Chamber could bring a conviction against me, and I believe there are no elements for proving genocide. As for Count 3, persecutions, the Prosecution did not choose between direct, individual responsibility, or guilt by association. Beginning with paragraph 14, items 3 through 6, the Prosecution claims that I supported and participated in the establishment and maintaining political and government organs and of the VRS, the TO, the MUP and Bosnian Serb paramilitary forces and volunteer units. They keep using the term "Bosnian Serb forces." This is another term that brings only confusion because Bosnian Serbs does not specify which forces were guilty of persecutions and arrests. The Prosecution calls everyone Bosnian Serb forces. For instance, the paramilitary formations in Bijeljina, Brcko, and Zvornik, for whose disbandment and arrest I engaged our own specialised brigade and requested even more specialised policemen and experienced fighters from Serbia. They call them also Bosnian Serb forces, although it is clear that Serb forces actually arrested them. As I've mentioned before, the Prosecution has also failed to prove that organs were established with the purpose that the Prosecution ascribes to them. The authorities were formed because it was our right according to international covenants on human rights. Every people has the right to self-organised, to foster its culture and identity and preserve its resources and assets. In the breakup of Yugoslavia, the Serbs made a minimal number of steps and the Prosecution has not proven that the authorities did exist. Now had been established with the intents that they claim they had. The Prosecution has failed to prove regarding persecution in various municipalities and everything that is covered by paragraphs, that is items 3 through 6, that there was a pattern of behaviour in Serb municipalities. There was no pattern, first of all, because in many municipalities nothing happened whatsoever; secondly, because the events in certain municipalities took place at different times. In some municipalities events started happening as late as two months after the war started and it was not up to the Serb side. Instead, it was both Muslims and Serbs in many municipalities that maintained peace for many months until an intervention occurred by central authorities in Sarajevo to start the fighting. The Prosecution did not prove any motivation or interest. The weaker Serb community in Bosnia holding, or rather, being stretched over 200 [as interpreted] kilometres of front line, what interest would they have in opening new front lines behind their lines? That would have been totally unreasonable. No motivation for that could be proved. I said 2.000 kilometres of front line, not 2 00. And when there were no troops behind our lines, because all of them were on the front line, why would we have started any new fighting with our compatriots of Muslim ethnicity? The Prosecution did not prove that any incident in municipalities happened at our initiative and in the absence of fighting. On the contrary, the witnesses have confirmed that in municipalities such as Sanski Most the evacuation of civilians in -- from combat areas such as Hrustovo, a witness confirmed that it was the Muslims who started shooting and there was fighting. The population was evacuated within the same municipality into a mixed Muslim-Serb village where there was no fighting, where everybody lived peacefully at the time, the mosque was not destroyed, this simply didn't happen. We see it on the screen now, a passage from the testimony. Yes. Here is a passage from the testimony of Dr. Mujadzic who confirms that in areas with a lower percentage of Muslims there were no problems. And he enumerates a large number of municipalities, 17 municipalities only in Krajina where there had been no problems. There was no pattern. To prove that there was one, the Prosecution would have to prove why measures were taken that were not of systemic nature. The first step that allegedly marks the beginning of a chain of criminal acts ascribed to me and other members of the JCE, the Prosecution points to so-called take-overs in municipalities. And in paragraph 105 of the pre-trial brief they specify immediately before the take-over of power, dismissals, discrimination, and other similar acts started. However, from my speech at the Assembly on the 25th of January, 1992, it is clearly obvious that I said we have legitimate and lawful authority over 70 per cent of the territory. And if you wanted to introduce a new kind of government you cannot introduce it there. The Prosecution has not proven that there was any take-over. Power was taken in some places because a lot of ex-communists remained in power after the new elections and it was necessary to introduce power after the elections. I claim that the same authorities were in place from 1992 to 1996 and there was no take-over. If we remember that the offer made was to have each ethnic community create its own municipalities with their own municipal organs of government, it is quite clear that this did not have anything to do with dismissals. The year was 1990. So the government was the same from 1990 until 1996. The elections were held in 1990. So everyone could have their own municipality, and it was therefore only natural that Muslim policemen would join the Muslim police station, but then they could also stay on, on the condition that they accepted Republika Srpska. We saw here Stojan Zupljanin's speech made on the 13th of May in Banja Luka. Since Banja Luka had not created ethnic municipalities, he said in that speech that almost all Muslims and Croats stayed on at the Banja Luka centre of the police and 50.000 inhabitants of Banja Luka applauded that. Now, where is intent there? Where is there any kind of intention of dismissing Muslims where there is a single municipality? That was not proven, that they had been dismissed. What was proven was that some did not want to acknowledge the authority of Republika Srpska, they did not want to take the solemn oath, they did not even want to go to the police station, but it has not been proven that they were dismissed an ethnic grounds. As far as persecution is concerned in Counts 3 to 6 there is a reference to detentions. However, the Prosecution did not prove that people were detained on the basis of their ethnic or religious affiliation. On the contrary, we see that detention had to do with investigation centres. A triage was carried out at these centres in terms of finding the persons who were suspected of having taken part in armed rebellion or, on the other hand, there were people who were mistakenly arrested, Serbs and Muslims were arrested by mistake. And such persons were released very quickly. Investigation centres were proclaimed camps in this indictment, like Keraterm, et cetera. Fifty-nine per cent of the people who were brought to these locations were released because they did not abide by the curfew, that's why they were arrested. But 59 per cent were released. It was established that 41 per cent had taken part in combat and committed crimes, therefore they were in prison. Of course in a situation where chaos prevailed and when there was a lack of communication with the central authorities, there were prisons, or rather, detention centres that had been established without the government knowing about this. We heard Prime Minister Djeric here describing the extent of the difficulty he had - he and the government - in terms of influencing what was happening on the ground because they did not have communication, they did not have access. However, even in these centres -- well, witnesses gave evidence to the contrary here, namely, that it was individuals that committed misdeeds. It was not organised and also these individuals did such things only when their immediate superiors were absent. For example, in Vogosca everybody was trying to conceal this from Branko Vlaco. No one dared say that they had done something. Then in Hadzici, Witness Music testified to the following: As soon as the hooligans got away, the guards took them out, they took them to a different room, not the one that had been affected by some yellow gas. Then in Omarska Muslim witnesses testified here to the following: Certain psychopaths among the guards mistreated detainees as soon as the investigators would leave. So this did not happen in front of the investigators. Also, a witness testified on page 19859 that they did not beat detainees before the commanders, their immediate superiors. So what happens in a civil war is what happens when brethren fight because Serbs consider Muslims to be their brothers. It has to be proven that that is part of the system and that the government and state stand behind that; that was not proven by the Prosecution. There is this absurd allegation in the indictment to the effect that I failed to notify government organs about misdeeds that were occurring in the field. However, what was proven here is that the president does not have investigation agencies of his own, that he is not capable of carrying out investigations, that it works the other way around, it is the state authorities, the government authorities, that should provide information to the president. It's not the other way around. How can the president know what is happening on the ground? I mean, when the government authorities are carrying out their work properly, then the president is not supposed to interfere. However, it has been proven here that I intervened or interfered only when it was necessary for me to intervene, namely, not to have persons released from custody and to speed up investigations. Many witnesses testified here stating that I did not meddle in the judiciary. I just asked for the judiciary to act in an expeditious manner, and also I did not want persons who had committed serious crimes to be set free. There are no finger-prints of mine on any misdeeds. Wherever I interfered, either following the intervention of international representatives or in any other way, this interference was on behalf of humanity, humaneness, lessening the suffering of all civilians irrespective of their ethnic background. So the Prosecution has not provided evidence on the basis of which the Trial Chamber could reach a decision amounting to a conviction with regard to Counts 3 to 6. Speaking of detentions, the Prosecution says that there was forced labour and so on. However, on page 19744 - I don't think that these were protected witnesses - they confirmed that work was voluntarily, not only at Manjaca but also at Batkovic, for instance. They could hardly wait in Batkovic to have an opportunity to work. For three months they would receive better food, they would bring food and alcohol to their colleagues, so it was not proven that this work or labour went outside the framework that is envisaged by law. And as a matter of fact, there even wasn't enough room for all of those who wanted to work to actually get this kind of work. As regards persecution, on page 19121, a witness testified stating that there were several obstacles on the path leading to freedom. Some people said that even 15 different certificates had to be handed in. Then also they testified to the effect that persons had to be bribed so that they could leave. Also that transport had to be paid for and the buses had to be awaited. Now, it is not only that many Serbs, Croats, and Muslims left before the war and during the first year of the war, but many changed their place of residence after the war. We saw the evidence adduced here by Ewa Tabeau, namely that between 1995 and 1997 there was a significant change in the ethnic picture because when people saw what kind of solution had been agreed upon, they decided to go to the entity in which their ethnic community was a majority. There was not a single place where there weren't Muslims and Croats, I mean there wasn't a single place in Republika Srpska where there weren't any Muslims and Croats. We saw the figures here. The Prosecution did not prove what kind of a difference there was between the Muslims and Croats who stayed on living there in peace throughout this period and, on the other hand, Croats who left Republika Srpska in different ways. There was no forcible deportation. The Prosecution did not prove any such thing. I have to say for the sake of the truth that like in many other cases language issues lead to the confusion. When somebody says that they were forced to leave and when we ask who it was that forced them, then we do not find a subject involved. Persons were compelled or forced to leave due to the situation, due to the conditions that prevailed. When you cannot identify who it was that forced them to leave, then it is developments as such that forced persons to leave. Now that we're dealing with detention facilities and persecution, we remember Eset Muracevic here who confirmed that out of 400 Muslims nine ended up in Kontiki, himself included, and he admitted that he smuggled weapons, or rather, that he was arming his community and carrying out preparations to fight. How can that be called persecution? I am completely leaving aside the fact that there is not a shred of evidence linking me to any of this and that that is the job of the president of the republic in any conceivable way. How can the president of the republic look into each and every corner and intervene? Least of all was there -- there was no evidence adduced to the effect that I intervened for the purpose of persecution. The Prosecution also says that I failed to take action in this kind and that I did not make efforts to have prosecution take place. First of all, the president only has the regular organs of the police and the judiciary, no organs of his own. The contrary has not been proven. I acted upon each and every credible information that I received about misdeeds that were committed. We heard Colm Doyle that he informed me on the 16th of August, 1992, about misdeeds that had been done, and on the 19th when I returned to Pale I made a decision annulling all of this. I even took action on the basis of information that was not all that credible, but still it was the Muslim propagandists that were fooling the international community in this way. And, therefore, I clashed with the army and the police because I was exerting pressure on them, telling them not to do something that they hadn't done in the first place. So the Prosecution did not prove any kind of concealment, not only on by part, they didn't prove that the police had concealed anything. We have seen a multitude of documents here. Each and every crime was documented, therefore it cannot be concealed because it would be dealt with at some point in time. If the perpetrator is known or accessible, these crimes were brought before a court even during the war itself. We heard people here from the judiciary who said that I did not intervene on behalf of the perpetrators; rather, I intervened in the opposite way. As for Counts 4, 5, and 6, that is to say extermination, murder, the Prosecution says different things here but they did not really prove that I had planned the extermination and murder of Muslims in various municipalities and then in Srebrenica and in Sarajevo. Because of a lack of evidence, the Prosecution is trying to gloss over the fact that there is no evidence to that and they keep saying that I must have contributed to this because there was a civil war going on. But they did not actually adduce any evidence. No mens rea on my part in terms of planning, aiding, abetting, instigating, committing murders, extermination, et cetera, not a shred of evidence. And then, as an alternative, they say that I knew or had reason to know that exterminations and murders would happen or had already happened and were committed by my subordinates. And they say that I took risks and that I continued to work on the accomplishment of these objectives in spite of that risk. We saw here that the Serb side did not need a war. The Serb side did not want to have a government that they did not accept imposed in its territory. It was absolutely unnecessary to resort to violence in order to attain the Serb strategic objectives. And, finally, it wasn't the Serbs who declared war on the Muslims; it was the Muslims who declared war on the Serbs. That was on the 20th of June, effectively from the 22nd of June. Serbia and Montenegro and Serbs in the Serb autonomous regions are declared the enemy. There is evidence showing that I spent all of 1992 trying to convince Izetbegovic that he should withdraw this and that we should have peace and seek a political solution. And now the Prosecution is saying that I should have told the Serbs, All right, all these things happening to you, let them happen, don't defend yourselves, because during your defence someone may commit a crime. But they would not have listened to me. It's not that I would have advised them to do that, but there are no instruments to prevent people from defending themselves. People who have experience from a war that had happened 50 years before that. The Prosecution still says in the indictment that I was the one who was trying to intimidate the Serbs, but these are open wounds. This is within living memory. There are people who are still alive and who were wounded and harmed in different ways in the Second World War, and no one needs to intimidate them. The Prosecution did not show that we wanted to impose our authority in any Muslim community, either in our own municipalities where Muslims were or in other areas. It's quite clear that the Muslims wanted to impose their authority on the Serbs. The Croats were free to express their own will, but the Muslims did that. There was evidence here that the Serbian community had nothing against Muslims and Islam, but we wanted them to remain and live in Yugoslavia. And evidence that it was not a matter of Muslims and Islam is the good co-operation with a number of people from the Muslim community who were not of an Islamic [as interpreted] or Muslim orientation. As for the establishment of the municipalities wherever there were conditions for that, this absolutely destroys the foundations for the assertions that we wanted to throw out Muslims and Croats from the territory of Republika Srpska. It should have been "fundamentalist" orientation instead of "Islamic" orientation. There's an error in the transcript. How was it possible to drive somebody out if you had a Muslim municipality of Bratunac and a Serb municipality of Bratunac? The very fact that the Serbs said that everyone should organise in their places of residence absolutely disqualifies any allegations about eventual intentions that Republika Srpska should be ethnically pure. Items or Counts 4, 5, and 6 have not been proved in any aspect. The Prosecution did not show that there was a systemic approach to the question of minorities in Republika Srpska from which these crimes would then result. Each municipality was specific and it had its own moment when peace turned into chaos, its own individual cause for that. There was no question of a decision by any state organ and there was no question of any initiative or order from any other place other than the fact that the circumstances in each municipality dictated what would happen. The Prosecution did not show that there was a pattern for the joint criminal enterprise to remove Muslims and Croats through killing. Prosecution witnesses confirmed that it was possible to live in Republika Srpska and that people were living in all settlements of Republika Srpska from the beginning until the end of the war and that this did not depend on the Serbian authorities. It was clearly proved that the disruption of the life of Muslim and Croat citizens could have happened by the immediate superior of any authority. Witnesses also confirmed here that the crucial fact was whether there was some fighting or not in a said municipality. Where there was no fighting the citizens were safe. The Prosecution did not show otherwise. As for deportations, Count 7 and 8, deportations, inhumane acts, these counts were also not proved in the sense that these things happened not with the initiative and will of the leadership but also with the knowledge and tacit approval of the state organs. Quite to the contrary, everywhere where authorities were established, such things were prevented, investigated, and punished or documented in order to be punished later. This is, once again, a question when we're talking about the crime of killing, the number of casualties, the numbers, and the Prosecution did not prove who did the killing and who were the victims. President of the republic or any state organ is unable to accept the fact that some Serbs killed some Muslims. Possibly yes, but this cannot be held to be the responsibility of the state organs or the bearers of state posts. We also saw that in Sanski Most the police investigated 30 incidents, and these were 30 incidents of violations against Croats and Muslims. None of them were left uninvestigated. And as Judge Draganovic said, prosecutions were possible on the basis of the investigations by the Serb authorities. I would now like to refer to Counts 9 and 10. The Prosecution gave up, abandoned, their assertions that the reasons for our acts in the Sarajevo area were the same as everywhere else: The removal of Muslims and Croats from the territories to -- which we claimed for ourselves. The Prosecution is aware and they did take into account that we did not dispose or intend to capture territories that were in the sector of Sarajevo, which is quite a considerable area, and where the majority population was Muslim. Quite the contrary. During the presentation of their case, the Prosecution proved that we did not claim nor undertake any offensives for the objective of capturing areas of Sarajevo except in one case for military reasons because we could not tolerate attacks from this area, Otes, anymore. A Muslim officer who testified here confirmed that the line of the front was more or less steady throughout the whole period and that the internal line of separation at the start of the war was 42 kilometres long and at the end of the war it was 64 kilometres long, which means that the Muslim side liberated or captured a part of the town and expanded this zone. Because by the very nature of the inner ring, had we advanced the confrontation line would have been shortened. This ring would have narrowed and the line of confrontation would have been shorter. The Muslims managed to extend the line of confrontation in the town from 42 to 64 kilometres, amounting to 22 kilometres of the front. It was not proven that it was our interest to conduct fighting in Sarajevo and it was not proven that we even initiated it. Even at the time when the Yugoslav People's Army was inert, people in neighbourhoods, in local communities set up a line of separation, literally defending their hearts. And except for this advance by the Muslim forces, this line remained steady more or less until the end of the war. We heard here from Prosecution witnesses, from representatives of the United Nations forces, that it was the military policy of the Serbian side in Sarajevo containment, containment of the large 1st Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. 17.000 Serbian soldiers, locals who lived there, they did not come from anywhere else, were protecting their neighbourhoods and containing 80.000 Muslim soldiers, preventing them from overrunning the Serbian part of Sarajevo and going to fight in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no siege even though the -- if it had been there it would have been legitimate. But there was no siege. Everybody was sieging everybody else, but the Serb locals became the Serbian army in defending their homes and their neighbourhoods. And now if we're not seeking and not intending to capture parts of Sarajevo and drive out Muslims and Croats, how - as is being ascribed to us for the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina - what would then have been the motive for us to terrorise Sarajevo? At that time there were between 50- to 70.000 Serbs living in Sarajevo who were not allowed to leave and who in racial terms are not any different from Serbs of the Muslim faith but are the same. It is being put forward now that we terrorised them by sniper fire. No incident in that sense was proved here beyond a reasonable doubt. We heard here that there were snipers who shot bursts of fire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... at this point we are not really concerned with proof beyond a reasonable doubt, not at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, it hasn't been proved at all. No incident has been proved. How can a sniper produce automatic fire? As in a case where one bullet shot a person in the tram and it was not visible. We heard some absolute gems as a result of investigations, where the source of -- we saw, for example, where directions are shifted by 90 degrees in order to prove that it was the Serbs who committed something. No incident actually was proved as having been committed by the Serb side. In conditions when Sarajevo was very militarised, something that was proved here, and where the military infrastructure and the military elements were intermingled with the civilians, something that General Dzambasovic confirmed here, that they did not have enough space to move away from their civilians. In conditions where the expenditure of large-calibre ammunition was equal or even greater on the Muslim side, the indictment still sticks to the position which it did not manage to prove that the Serbs fired more than the Muslims did or that the Serbs would fire first without any provocation or without any context of defence. The Prosecution did not manage to prove that this was unilateral fire. They did not manage to prove that the Serbian side fired indiscriminately. The Prosecution did not show or proffer evidence that the return fire from the Serbian side was indiscriminate. Not only was the Muslim military infrastructure all over the place, but also there was the fact of mobile mortars. So there was no evidence that the Serbian side fired indiscriminately and without any military cause. Of course the question of ammunition expenditure showed that, for example, the Muslim forces fired a large number of shells, only a part of which targeted or hit Serbian territory. The Prosecution did not then manage to show where these other shells fell and they did not differentiate between what was Serb shelling and what was a Muslim shelling. We have seen here quite failed investigation, even grotesque-sounding investigations, where the trajectory was not established horizontally or vertically, but one would just come to the window and look at Serb positions and say, Yes, that's where the fire came from. This was something that was completely unproved. The Prosecution did not manage to tell who committed the crimes even in the case of Serbs. They did not manage to identify exactly which Serbs possibly fired. The Prosecution refers to Sarajevo forces as the perpetrators of various crimes. Which Sarajevo forces? There were 5- or 6.000 Serbian soldiers involved with Sarajevo and some 10.000 who were involved in the Central Bosnia front in the town. The front was 40 kilometres broad. In the town itself there were 40- to 60.000 Muslim soldiers at any given time. These were also Sarajevo forces. The Prosecution did not manage to prove that the Serbs carried out military unjustified actions in the Sarajevo sector and did not manage to prove that Sarajevo was a civilian zone nor did they manage to prove that the civilians were the target of any given military action by the Serb side. Quite the contrary. It was shown that the town was full of trenches, that the line of separation of the Serbs and the Muslims was 40 kilometres long, sometimes just a few metres apart. And what came out was quite opposite from the assertions of the Prosecution, and that is that there were Muslim sniper nests and also the international representatives were convinced that the Muslim side also fired on its own people. In conditions where we have mobile artillery heavy weaponry and mortars, in conditions where we have indications, well-grounded indications that there was fire on their own people, the Prosecution is then obliged to precisely prove that something that was fired was fired from the Serbian side and that it was fired with the intention alleged in the indictment. We did not, however, see such proof. International representatives here testified for the Prosecution and confirmed that the Muslim tactics in the Sarajevo area was to show the worst possible situation, and they did everything they could to secure international military intervention. In conditions of this confirmed tactics, the worst, the better, the Prosecution did not manage to show who did what and with which motive. They did not manage to prove that and they did not manage to isolate exactly what it was that the Serbian side did. The shooting that we saw in the Sarajevo sector was mutual. Had the Serb side been firing at the city and at civilian facilities indiscriminately, you would have ruins that would be worse than those in Dresden or Mostar. We saw aerial footage of such results. Compared to such destruction, Sarajevo was not even scratched. I kindly ask for your indulgence for a moment. Excellencies, as for the position on humanitarian issues, the Prosecution did not manage to prove that I had a negative attitude towards civilian matters or the welfare of civilians of any ethnicity. I did not interfere in these matters unless this intervention was asked of me. When I was asked to do so and evidence was shown here that my intervention was always on behalf and for the benefit of the flow of humanitarian aid in order to ease the position of civilians. Each intervention was always of that kind. Not only did I issue a lot of general-type documents in order to prevent suffering, not only did I intervene frequently, perhaps even without justification with my own army, scolding them and attacking them frequently without justification, I also reacted to any report from international factors that they noticed that something was being held up somewhere, that aid was not arriving. I would always intervene. Wherever I left any traces, all of these traces would be in order to support humanitarian aspects and for the benefit of civilians. Gentlemen, we saw Sarajevo. Any drop of water that Sarajevo received, except for a small spring, came from the Serbian side. Whenever we had water, they also had water. The Prosecution did not prove that we sabotaged the civilian life in Sarajevo. The Prosecution did not prove that it was our interest to have fighting in Sarajevo, quite the opposite. There was evidence that we often proposed that militarisation of Sarajevo and placing Sarajevo under UN administration -- the other side would not accept that. But we have quite convincing proof that the international factors confirmed this as being our position. Everything that was received for the civilians came through Serbian territory. A witness from a humanitarian organisation confirmed here that there was an average of 700 transporters and trucks every day on the roads of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Except for a narrow area going along the sea, all these transports went through the territory of Republika Srpska. The proportion of hindered inspected and intercepted convoys due to some irregularity is negligible compared to the total number of convoys that arrived. It has been shown and proven that my position was that we should not wage war using electricity, water, gas and food. It has been shown that the Serb side was forthcoming and provided its compatriots in the Muslim part of Sarajevo with aid without any discrimination. Look at the testimony of General, I believe, Milovanovic. He said he used my name to facilitate the passage of convoys and the observance of his own orders. If he had any problems with the army who protested why the Muslims were getting food when they had none, he would drop my name and that helped convoys pass through. Thousands of flights landed at Sarajevo airport. We controlled that airport; it was on Serbian land. We controlled it and we made it possible to use that airport to provide Sarajevo with humanitarian aid, although of course they were able to introduce whole units and war equipment through the tunnel, they also used humanitarian convoys for that. But the fact is everything that was not air-lifted to facilitate the civilian life in Sarajevo came through the Serbian territory 365 days a year. And the Prosecution simply cannot prove that the Serbian side - and especially me - hindered humanitarian efforts or that I contributed in any way to the suffering of civilians. On the contrary, all the evidence shows that I did all I could to ease their situation. Of course there remains the fact that it was very difficult to command and control a popular army consisting of soldiers who are local residents. Here's a passage of one testimony: "No, I haven't seen any directives straight from the higher level." General Razek confirms there were difficulties in command and control and that it was not difficult to keep things under control on the ground. General Razek confirmed that this was a civil war where not only armies fired at each other but civilians against civilians, farmers against farmers. And now we see that the developments in Syria are very much like the events in Bosnia. We hear that from American generals. They say that one village is fighting another. And how could the Prosecution have been even expected to prove the responsibility of the central authorities of the republic under circumstances where there were no professional armies, where everybody had their own army. On the contrary, it was proven that in places where the state has a presence, where the Serbian forces were really present, the crime rate was the lowest. The Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We wanted to show to you a lot more than we are able to within this limited time, but we are convinced that being a professional Trial Chamber rather than a jury you realise yourself how many things, how many allegations by the Prosecution, remain unproven and how many things are proven to the contrary, in fact. There is a kind of virtual bridge that the Prosecution is trying to use to link some war events to me, presenting them as a product of my criminal intentions, like that we wanted to create a homogenous and ethnically pure Serbian republic. That has not been proven. And if that has not been proven, the whole indictment should collapse. It has not been proven that our intentions were illegitimate, there is no evidence that our intentions could only have been realised through war and violence. Our objectives were possible to achieve politically. They were recognised by the international community and they were sanctioned, codified in all the treaties and agreements, and finally formulated in the Dayton Accords and that will remain so for all times. They are simply grounded in our rights. If a war was detrimental and unneeded by anyone, those were the Serbs. But the Prosecution didn't even bother to try to prove this, the existence of this narrow bridge. The Prosecution failed to lay a foundation for the indictment let alone prove its allegations in it. I will not use up any more of your time, and I will kindly ask Mr. Robinson to present our position on Count 16 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 11, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to take about 20 minutes, so I think we can continue and finish before lunch, but I do have some copies for the interpreters of our slides that I'm going to use during this part of the presentation. I hadn't had a chance to distribute it earlier, so if that could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we go from Count 1 where there was a plethora of jurisprudence to Count 11 where there's basically no jurisprudence on the issue of whether the detention of UN personnel constituted a hostage-taking. So we look at Count 11 and Count 11 simply charges hostage-taking in violation of Article 3 of the ICTY Statute. Article 3 of the ICTY Statute encompasses conduct that is prohibited By Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. And finally, when we get to Common Article 3, it indicates that: "Each party to the conflict shall be bound to apply as a minimum the following provisions: First, that persons taking no active part in the hostilities, including members of armed forces who have laid down their arms and those placed hors de combat by sickness, wounds, detention, or any other cause shall in all circumstances be treated humanely." And among the acts that are prohibited by Common Article 3 are the taking of hostages. The elements of hostage taking can be found in the ICC elements of crimes because they've never specifically been enumerated in ICTY jurisprudence and we believe that basically these elements would be the same with maybe some slight issue about one. The first three elements are that the perpetrator seized, detained, or otherwise held hostage one or more persons; that the perpetrator threatened to kill, injure, or continue to detain such person or persons; and that the perpetrator intended to compel a third party to refrain or act in an explicit condition for the safety or release of such person or persons. These three elements aren't really the focus of my submission in this case. It's the fourth and fifth elements where we think that there are matters of importance. The fourth element is that at the time the person or persons were protected under one or more of the Geneva Conventions; and fifth, that the perpetrator was aware of the factual circumstances that provided that protected status. And so, the issue in our case as we see it is: Were the UN personnel who were detained persons taking no active part in the hostilities, such as to render them protected persons under Common Article 3? And so it depends -- the answer to this question depends on whether the UN was engaged as combatants at the time their personnel were detained. And you recall the facts of the hostage-taking incident, which were essentially that General Rupert Smith had warned the Bosnian Serbs that unless they returned certain heavy weapons to the exclusion zone around Sarajevo, he would authorise NATO to commence air-strikes. And when the Bosnian Serbs did not return all of the heavy weapons to the exclusion zone, he authorised an air-strike on a separate target; that is, the ammunition depot in Pale. And that ammunition depot was hit by NATO air-strikes on the afternoon of the 25th of May, 1995, and on the morning of the 26th of May, 1995, and following those air-strikes, personnel of the United Nations who were in Serb-controlled territory were detained. So those are the facts, and the question is: What was the status of those persons at the time they were detained? We believe that that's answered by a Convention on the Safety of United Nations and Associated Personnel that has been come into force and was promulgated through the United Nations at the beginning of 1995 and came into force sometime later, after this incident took place. And it provides for the protection of United Nations personnel in combat areas and in areas where they're serving as peacekeepers, but it indicates that this convention shall not apply to a United Nations operation authorised by the Security Council as an enforcement action under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations, and there is no doubt that what was authorised in Bosnia was an enforcement action under Chapter VII. All the UN resolutions are replete with references to Chapter VII. And then it goes on to say: "In which any of the personnel are engaged as combatants against organised armed forces and to which the law of international armed conflict applies." Now, in the ICC they dealt with a situation where an accused was charged with an attack on peacekeepers, not hostage-taking, but a different violation. And that happened in Darfur and in that case, the Abu Garda case, the Pre-Trial Chamber hearing the confirmation of charges decided that there was a distinction between peacekeeping operations which only use self-defence and so-called peace-enforcement missions authorised under Chapter VII which have a mandate or are authorised to use force beyond self-defence in order to achieve their objective. And that's what we had in Bosnia, where Colonel Rupert Smith or General Rupert Smith was authorised to call in air-strikes, not in self-defence but to "enforce the mandate of the United Nations." And in the ICC the Chamber said that personnel involved in peacekeeping operations enjoy protection from attacks unless and for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities or in combat-related activities. And the majority finds that that protection does not cease if such persons only use armed force in the exercise of their right to self-defence, which is what took place in Sudan. But in our case, General Rupert Smith acknowledged that the bombing of the Pale ammunition depot was not in self-defence. You'll find that on page 11873 of the transcript, and he agreed that the personnel carrying out the air-strikes were combatants. You'll find that at page 11880 of the transcripts. We also have evidence of the positive impact that air-strike had on the war effort of the Muslims and the UN reported that in Exhibit D1176 at page 61 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just a moment, there's no Serb translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think it has now been completed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah. You have been -- you stopped to the issue of the benefits for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. General Smith made the distinction that NATO was a combatant but the UN was not, and that's legally incorrect. Judge Christopher Greenwood in an article he wrote before he became a judge at the International Court of Justice said that: "Even if it could be argued that only the NATO air-strikes and not the ground operations of UNPROFOR itself reached the level of an armed conflict, that would not be sufficient to prevent Article 2(2)," and he's referring to the convention on the safety of UN personnel that I showed you earlier, "from removing the protection of the safety convention from UNPROFOR personnel, since Article 2(2) applies to the entirety of a United Nations operation if any of the personnel involved operate as combatants against organised armed forces in circumstances to which the law of international armed conflict applies." The International Law Commission has a document called The Articles of Responsibility of International Organisations, and at Article 16(2) of that document it provides that an organisation is responsible if it authorises or recommends another international organisation to commit an act. And here General Smith testified that the NATO air-strikes were at his request. You will find that at page 11494 of the transcript and in his book which is in evidence as Exhibit D1009 at page 354 he said that the UN went from confrontation to conflict with the Bosnian Serbs when he ordered those air-strikes. It's also well-established that all active-duty members of an armed force are considered combatants, regardless of their actual duties. And General Smith testified that all of the UN personnel who were detained were on active duty. And you can see here references to the ICRC, the Red Cross, in which they have provided that all active-duty personnel of a belligerent are considered to be persons taking direct part in hostilities. Now, what about the question of whether these UN personnel could be considered hors de combat as a result of their detention? So, for example, you heard the facts from Captain Patrick Rechner who testified that he and other members of the UN military observers were at their home or at their office home in Pale when members of the Serb forces came in, detained them, and threatened to kill them if the air-strikes weren't stopped. And the question is whether or not by virtue of that detention they became -- went from combatants to protected persons. The answer, we submit, is no. Because otherwise the crime could not be committed, the crime of hostage-taking, could simply not be committed against anyone other than a protected person if everyone who was detained as part of the hostage-taking automatically has their status transferred from combatant to a person hors de combat, and that would make those elements, that the person has to be a protected person and that the accused or the perpetrator has to know about that status, to be completely redundant under the Statute. In addition, the crime of hostage-taking according to some ICTY jurisprudence occurs at the time of detention. In the Blaskic and Kordic case, the Trial Chambers held that the Prosecution must establish that at the time of the supposed detention the allegedly censurable act was perpetrated in order to obtain a concession or gain an advantage. Now, these cases arose out of a very different factual circumstance than the one we have here. In that case there were already about 2.000 prisoners that were under the Croats' control. Those were either civilians or combatants who had been held for quite a long time. So those who were combatants were, in fact, hors de combat by the time that the threat was made. But in this case, the evidence is that the detention was directly linked to the threat and for the purpose of asking that the air-strikes stop. And therefore, it cannot be said that those UN personnel who were detained were hors de combat at the time of detention. Therefore, the element that requires that the victim of hostage-taking be a protected person under the Geneva Convention has not been established. In addition, the element that the perpetrator be aware of the factual circumstances that established that protective status is also not satisfied. The record is replete with consistent statements by Dr. Karadzic that the UN personnel had been detained as prisoners of war before, during, and after the hostage crisis. While the subsequent use of prisoners as human shields may well have constituted a crime, that crime is not charged in this indictment. Therefore, because there is no evidence upon which the Trial Chamber could conclude that each of the essential elements of Count 11 have been established, it should enter a judgement of acquittal for the charge of hostage-taking. Mr. President and members of the Trial Chamber, we thank you for your attention to our submissions today. I'd like to also thank many of the legal interns whose research contributed to our submissions, and that concludes our motion. Thank you.
